Food does not go bad by magic. Every spoiled tomato, sour pot of stew or weevil-filled bag of beans has a cause you can name. When you know the cause, you can choose a method that stops it. This first lesson gives you that understanding, so every later lesson makes sense.
A cartoon microbe
Most fast spoilage at home is caused by tiny living things you cannot see: bacteria, yeasts and moulds.
Five causes of spoilage

**Microbes.** Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are tiny living things on hands, surfaces, water, soil and the food itself. They feed on food and multiply. Some only change taste and smell. Others, such as the bacteria behind food poisoning, can make people ill without changing how the food looks.

**Enzymes.** These are natural substances inside food that keep working after harvest or slaughter. They make a cut yam or apple turn brown, a banana go soft and black, and vegetables lose colour in a freezer if they were not blanched first.

**Air (oxygen).** Air slowly reacts with fats and oils. That is why groundnuts, crayfish, palm oil and fried snacks can develop a sharp, stale smell called rancidity. Air also lets moulds grow on the surface of food.
**Pests.** Weevils, beetles, moths, cockroaches, ants, rats and lizards eat food and leave droppings, hairs and eggs that carry germs.

**Physical damage.** Bruises, cracks and cuts break the natural skin of fruit, vegetables, eggs and grains. Microbes and air enter through the wound, and the item spoils days earlier than its neighbours.
What microbes need

Microbes need the same few things almost all the time: **food, water, warmth, time** and, for most of them, **air**. Take one away and they slow down or stop. This is the idea behind every method in this course. Drying and salting take away water. Refrigeration and freezing take away warmth. Pickling and fermenting make the food too sour (acidic) for harmful bacteria. Sugar in jam ties up water. Sealing takes away air, but be careful: one dangerous bacterium, *Clostridium botulinum*, grows only where there is **no** air, so sealing alone can make some foods more dangerous, not less. Lesson 3 explains this in detail.

Warmth matters a lot in Nigeria. The World Health Organization (WHO) Five Keys to Safer Food poster marks the range between **5°C and 60°C** as the danger zone, where bacteria multiply quickly. A kitchen afternoon in most Nigerian towns sits inside that zone. That is why cooked rice left on the stove overnight, or fish left in a bowl after market, can become unsafe even when it smells fine.

Worked example: sorting a basket of tomatoes
For example, Bisi buys a basket of 60 tomatoes for about ₦18,000 (an approximate price; market prices change weekly). On the bus home some get squeezed.
She tips the basket gently onto a clean tray, never leaving the tomatoes packed tight in the heat.
She finds 9 tomatoes with soft or split skin. That is 9 ÷ 60 = 15% of the basket.
Each tomato cost her about ₦18,000 ÷ 60 = ₦300, so the damaged ones are worth about 9 × ₦300 = ₦2,700.

She checks the tray every morning and moves any newly softening tomato into the cooking pile.

A big basket is cheaper per tomato only if you can use or preserve it before it spoils. If your space and time allow you to handle only half a basket, buying half is often the cheaper choice.

The hurdle idea

Food scientists talk about **hurdles**. Each method is a hurdle a microbe has to jump. One very high hurdle, like hard freezing, can be enough on its own. But several smaller hurdles together are often safer and give better taste. Smoked fish, for example, is salted (hurdle one), partly dried by the heat (hurdle two), coated with smoke (hurdle three), and then stored in a dry, airy place (hurdle four). Pepper sauce is cooked (one), acidified with vinegar (two), packed hot into clean jars (three) and refrigerated after opening (four).

Questions to ask before you choose
**What is the food?** Acidic foods such as most fruit behave very differently from low-acid foods such as fish, meat, beans and most vegetables.
**How long must it keep?** Two days for a party, two weeks for the family, or six months for sale?
**What equipment and power do you have?** A freezer is only as good as your electricity or generator hours. Sun, salt, vinegar and sugar work without power.
**Will you sell it?** Food for sale must be consistent, labelled and, for packaged products, registered with NAFDAC. Start with methods you can repeat exactly.
**What does your household or customer like?** Preserved food that nobody eats is still waste.
Worked example: one weekend, three surplus foods

For example, Halima comes home from her cousin's farm with 6 kg of ripe mango, 3 kg of fresh tilapia and a large bundle of ugwu. She has one empty freezer shelf, two mesh drying trays and about 6 hours of power a day.
Fish spoils fastest, so she deals with it first. She guts and cleans it, divides it into 500 g packs, which gives 3,000 g ÷ 500 g = 6 packs, labels them and freezes them flat so they freeze quickly.
Ugwu wilts within a day or two. She blanches it, squeezes out water and freezes it in 4 small soup-sized bags on the same shelf.
Mango keeps a few days if it is not bruised. Each tray holds about 1.5 kg of slices, so 6 kg needs 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 tray-loads. With 2 trays she needs 2 sunny days.
She eats or shares the softest mangoes now instead of drying them, because bruised fruit dries poorly.
Everything is protected within two days, the freezer is used only for the foods that need it, and the free sun does the work for the mango.
Preserving does not repair spoiled food

Every method only slows or stops future spoilage. It cannot make bad food good again. Drying a mouldy tomato or smoking a fish that already smells gives you a spoiled product that lasts longer. Start with fresh, sound food every time.

Preserving gives food a long life. That is good for your pocket, but it also gives any harmful microbe a long time to grow if the process was wrong. This lesson sets the safety rules for the rest of the course. Read it carefully, and come back to it whenever you try a new recipe.
A yellow warning sign
A few clear safety rules protect your family and your customers from the rare but serious dangers of preserved food.
The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
The World Health Organization teaches five simple keys. They apply to preserving just as much as to cooking.
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
Check all five keys before you start any preserving job.

**Keep clean.** Wash your hands before handling food and often during preparation, and after using the toilet. Wash and sanitise surfaces and equipment. Protect food and kitchen areas from insects, pests and other animals.

**Separate raw and cooked.** Keep raw meat, poultry and seafood away from other foods. Use separate knives and boards for raw foods, and store foods in containers so raw and prepared foods do not touch.
**Cook thoroughly.** Bring soups and stews to the boil so they reach 70°C. Reheat cooked food thoroughly.

**Keep food at safe temperatures.** Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Refrigerate cooked and perishable food promptly, preferably below 5°C. Keep hot food above 60°C. Do not store food too long even in the fridge, and do not thaw frozen food at room temperature.
**Use safe water and raw materials.** Use safe or treated water. Choose fresh, wholesome food, wash fruit and vegetables, and do not use food beyond its expiry date.
Botulism: the hidden danger in sealed jars and oil

Botulism is a rare but very serious illness caused by a toxin from the bacterium *Clostridium botulinum*. WHO explains that this bacterium can only grow **without oxygen**, and it **will not grow in acidic conditions (pH below 4.6)**. Its spores survive ordinary boiling. WHO names **home-made canned, preserved or fermented foods** as a common source, including low-acid preserved vegetables, and fish that has been fermented, salted or smoked.

Think about what that means in a Nigerian kitchen. A sealed jar, a tightly tied nylon bag or a layer of oil on top of food all shut out air. If the food under the seal is **low-acid** (vegetables, garlic, ginger, onions, pepper paste without vinegar, beans, fish, meat) and it sits at room temperature, the conditions suit this bacterium. The food may look, smell and taste normal.
Low-acid foods in oil or sealed jars

Never store raw or cooked garlic, ginger, onions, herbs, vegetables, pepper paste, fish or meat under oil, or in a sealed jar, at room temperature unless you are following a tested recipe that makes it acidic or uses proper pressure canning. Oil on top does not preserve food; it removes air and can help botulism bacteria grow. Make oil-based mixtures in small amounts, keep them in the fridge, and use them up quickly. Do not sell home-made garlic or ginger in oil.

WHO notes that symptoms usually begin 12 to 36 hours after eating (sometimes 4 hours to 8 days) with marked tiredness, weakness and dizziness, followed by blurred vision, dry mouth and difficulty swallowing and speaking. It can paralyse the muscles used for breathing. Anyone with these signs after eating preserved food needs a hospital at once. WHO also states that the toxin is destroyed by boiling (for example, an internal temperature above 85°C for 5 minutes or longer), but this does not make it acceptable to eat a suspicious jar: throw it away.
Honey and babies
WHO warns parents and caregivers not to feed honey to babies under 1 year old, because honey can carry botulism spores.

Worked example: a risky product idea
For example, Amaka runs a small provisions shop in Enugu. Customers ask for ready-made blended garlic and ginger in oil, and she plans to make 20 jars a week to sell from the shelf.
She checks the food: garlic and ginger are low-acid. That is one warning.
She checks the packing: a layer of oil and a sealed lid shut out air. That is a second warning.
She checks the storage: her shelf is at room temperature for weeks. That is a third warning.
Three warnings together match the conditions WHO describes for botulism, so she drops the idea.
Instead she sells sun-dried ginger slices and a vinegar-based pepper sauce made from a tested recipe, which are safer at room temperature.
Amaka protects her customers and her shop's name, and still meets the demand with two safer products.

Drying is the cheapest preservation method in a sunny country. It needs no electricity, and dried food is light, so it takes little space. But careless drying gives dusty, mouldy food that spoils in weeks. This lesson shows you how to dry three very different foods well: tomatoes (juicy and acidic), leafy vegetables (thin and delicate) and mango (sweet and fleshy).
A ripe red tomato
Tomatoes are the classic drying crop: cheap and plentiful in the glut season, costly in the scarce months.
Rules for every drying job

**Raised and covered.** Dry food on mesh or woven trays raised off the ground, never on a mat or zinc sheet on the floor. Cover with clean net or mosquito mesh to keep off flies, birds, dust and lizards.
**Air above and below.** Mesh lets air pass under the food, so it dries on both sides at once.
**Single layer, even size.** Pieces should not touch. Cut everything to about the same thickness so it all dries at the same rate.
**Bring it in at night.** Night air is damp and food left out takes back water. Bring trays inside, covered, and put them out again in the morning.
**Clean hands, clean water.** Wash produce in safe water and wash your hands and knives before cutting.
A simple solar dryer

A solar dryer is a box or tent with a clear plastic or glass cover, a dark surface inside to absorb heat, and air vents low on one side and high on the other. Warm air rises through the food and leaves through the top vent, carrying water away. It dries faster than open sun, protects food from rain and insects, and keeps colour better. You can build one from wood, mesh and clear polythene. Keep the vents covered with net so insects cannot enter.

Pieces on the edge of a tray dry faster than those in the middle, so some may still hold water when the batch feels dry. Before you pack for long storage, **condition** the batch: fill a clean, dry glass jar about two-thirds full, close it and shake it once a day for about a week. If drops of water form inside the jar, or pieces stick together, spread the food out and dry it more. If it stays loose and dry, it is ready to pack.

Salt has preserved fish and meat for thousands of years. Salt pulls water out of the flesh and leaves too little free water for most spoilage bacteria. It also firms the flesh and adds flavour. But salt works slowly from the outside in, and WHO lists salted fish among the foods that can carry botulism when the process goes wrong. So salting is always done with care, and almost always followed by drying, smoking or cold storage.

Step by step: dry-salted fish
Start with very fresh fish. Bright clear eyes, red gills, firm flesh and a clean sea or river smell. Salting will not rescue fish that is already stale.
Gut the fish, remove the gills and wash the belly cavity well with safe water. The gut is the part that spoils fastest.
Split thick fish open along the back or belly, or cut deep slashes, so salt can reach the thickest part.
Use clean, dry food-grade salt. Rub it into every surface and fill the belly cavity.
Layer fish and salt in a clean plastic or food-grade container, skin side down, with salt between each layer and a thick layer on top. Cover and keep it in the coolest shaded place you have.
Liquid (pickle) will collect as salt draws water out. Drain it as your tested family or extension recipe directs.
Rinse off loose salt and dry the fish on raised, covered racks in the sun or a solar dryer, bringing it in at night, until it is firm and dry right through.
Making a full-strength brine

To make a strong brine without measuring tools, stir salt into clean water until no more dissolves and some salt stays at the bottom. A saturated brine like this is as salty as plain water can get, so the strength is the same every time.

How do you know the salting worked? Well salted and dried fish is firm, pale or golden, and smells clean and salty. The flesh near the bone is as firm as the outside. Warning signs are a soft, wet or pink centre, a sour or rotten smell when you press the thickest part, or slime on the surface. Fish with these signs is not safe to store and should be thrown away, not re-salted.
Salting meat

Meat is salted in a similar way, but it must be cut into thin strips first so salt and heat reach the centre quickly. Northern Nigerian **kilishi** is a familiar example: thin sheets of beef dried, coated with spiced groundnut paste, dried again and roasted. If you salt and dry meat at home, cut it thin, keep it covered from flies, dry it fully, and cook it thoroughly before eating.

Smoked fish is part of almost every Nigerian kitchen, from stockfish-style dried catfish to smoked mackerel and bonga. Hot-smoking does three jobs together: the heat cooks the fish, the warm air dries it, and the smoke leaves a coating that adds flavour and helps slow surface mould. Done well, hard-smoked fish keeps for weeks in a dry place. Done badly, it is burnt outside, wet inside, and spoils quickly.
A whole fish
Small and medium fish such as catfish, mackerel and bonga are commonly hot-smoked in West Africa.

Preparing the fish
Use only fresh fish. Smoking does not repair stale fish.
Gut the fish and remove gills. Wash in safe water. For catfish, scrub off the slime.
For thick fish, make deep cuts across the body so heat and smoke reach the bone.
Brine the fish in a full-strength salt solution, or rub with salt, for flavour and to firm the surface. Drain well.
Arrange fish on clean wire racks in one layer, not touching, so smoke and air can circulate.
Running the smoke

Hot-smoking is a slow process with three stages. First, gentle heat and good airflow dry the wet surface. Next, higher heat cooks the fish through: the flesh should turn opaque and come away firmly from the bone. Last, low heat over many hours drives out water for long keeping. Turn and rotate racks so fish near the fire does not burn while the top rack stays wet.

How do you check that the fish is cooked and dry? Break open the thickest fish on the lowest-heat part of the rack. Cooked flesh is opaque all the way to the bone, with no pink, glassy or watery parts. Hard-smoked fish should feel light for its size, firm when pressed, and sound dry when two fish are tapped together. If the centre still feels soft and damp, the fish needs more time on low heat, not more fire.

Use dry, untreated hardwood, coconut husk or charcoal. **Never** burn plastic, tyres, painted, varnished or chemically treated wood: they release poisonous smoke that settles on the food.
Keep fish well above the flames. Fat dripping into an open flame flares up and blackens fish, and burnt, charred fish carries more harmful smoke substances.
Aim for a steady smoulder, not a blaze. Control heat by adding or removing fuel and opening or closing vents.
Protect your lungs, eyes and family

Wood smoke harms the lungs and eyes, especially when you work beside it for many hours every week. Smoke outdoors or under an open shed, with your back to the wind, never inside a closed kitchen or bedroom. Use a smoker or kiln with a chimney that carries smoke up and away from your face. Keep children and babies away from the smoking area, keep water or sand nearby for fire, and wear cotton clothes, not synthetic fabric that melts.

Rukayat knows that each kilogram of her hard-smoked catfish costs about ₦11,300 before packaging and labour, and that she loses about two-thirds of the weight as water.

Let fish cool completely before packing, or it will sweat and grow mould.
Store hard-smoked fish in clean cartons, baskets or paper, in a dry, airy place off the floor. Do not seal it in plastic while it is still warm.
Check weekly. If you find damp patches or beginning mould, or small beetles and larvae, remove affected fish. Lightly re-smoking or re-drying sound fish restores dryness.

Throw away fish that smells rotten, feels slimy, or has mould deep in the flesh. WHO lists smoked fish among foods linked to botulism when badly processed, so never seal soft-smoked fish airtight at room temperature.

Fermentation is one of Africa's oldest food skills. Ogi (akamu), fufu, garri, iru (dawadawa), ogiri and nono are all fermented. In a good ferment, friendly bacteria, mostly lactic acid bacteria, eat some of the sugar in the food and turn it into acid. The food becomes sour, and that sourness makes life hard for many harmful bacteria. You are not killing microbes; you are helping the right ones win.
An ear of maize
Maize, sorghum and millet are steeped, milled and soured to make ogi.

The friendly bacteria need a fair start: clean grain or vegetables, safe water, clean containers and the right amount of time. If the start is dirty, or the water is unsafe, unwanted microbes can win instead. That is why the WHO key **use safe water and raw materials** matters so much here: ogi is made almost entirely of water.
Making ogi step by step
**Clean the grain.** Pick out stones, shrivelled, discoloured or mouldy grains. Mouldy maize can carry aflatoxin, a mould poison; washing or souring does not remove it.
**Steep.** Cover the grain with plenty of safe water in a clean, covered bucket. Leave it for about one to three days until a grain crushes easily between your fingers.
**Wet-mill.** Drain and grind the soft grain at the mill or with a blender. Some households add ginger, cloves or pepper for flavour.
**Sieve.** Mix the paste with safe water and pass it through a fine sieve or clean cloth, squeezing well. Keep the white liquid; the husk left behind can be used for animal feed.
**Settle and sour.** Cover the white liquid and leave it to settle for about one to three days. It will smell pleasantly sour as the starch sinks to the bottom.
**Pour off the top water.** The thick white sediment is ogi. Keep it as it is, wrap it in leaves or clean food bags, or press out the water to make a firmer cake.

In hot weather it sours further each day. Keep it in the fridge if you have power, and make amounts your household or customers will use within a few days.
Use a clean, dry spoon every time. Never put your hand into the container.

A good ferment bubbles gently and smells clean and sour. When it is as sour as you like, move it to the fridge.

Vinegar pickles and pepper sauces that stay safe

Pickling preserves food with acid. In a vinegar pickle you add the acid yourself. WHO explains that botulism bacteria **will not grow in acidic conditions below pH 4.6**, so enough acid, spread evenly through every piece, is the safety line. Onions, cucumbers, carrots, garden eggs and peppers all pickle well and sell well beside suya, rice and small chops.
A green cucumber
Crisp vegetables like cucumber, onion and carrot become pickles when vinegar makes them acidic.
The three pickling rules
The US National Center for Home Food Preservation, a widely used university reference for home preserving, gives three rules that matter most:
**Use vinegar of 5% acidity.** Check the label. White distilled vinegar of 5% acidity is the standard. Do not use vinegar of unknown strength.

**Do not change the proportions** of vinegar, water and vegetables in a tested recipe. Adding extra water or more vegetables weakens the acid. The guide states there must be a minimum, even level of acid throughout the product to prevent botulinum bacteria.
**Use pickling or canning salt** if the recipe asks for salt. The anti-caking additives in some table salts make the brine cloudy.
Preparing vegetables for pickling
Choose firm, fresh vegetables with no soft spots. Pickling will not firm up a limp cucumber or rescue a bruised onion.
Wash them well in safe water, scrubbing off soil, and trim away the flower end of cucumbers, which can soften pickles.
Cut pieces to an even size so the vinegar reaches the centre of every piece at the same rate.
Pack vegetables firmly but not crushed, so the liquid can flow around every piece and cover the top completely.
Wear gloves when cutting hot peppers such as scotch bonnet (ata rodo), and keep your hands away from your eyes.
Sterilising jars
Wash jars and lids in hot soapy water and rinse well.
Place the jars in a large pot, cover them fully with water and boil for 10 minutes.
Lift them out with clean tongs, drain upside down on a clean cloth, and fill while still hot.
Do not dry the inside with a towel; let them air-dry from their own heat.
Refrigerator pickles and shelf pickles

A **refrigerator pickle** is made by pouring a hot vinegar mixture over prepared vegetables in clean jars, cooling, and keeping the jars in the fridge. It is quick and suits small batches, but it is not shelf-stable. A **shelf pickle** is processed after filling in a boiling-water bath for a set time, following a tested recipe exactly. If you have not done that, treat your pickle as a fridge product and label it **Keep refrigerated**.

A **vinegar pepper sauce** is blended pepper, onion and spices cooked with vinegar to a tested recipe, poured hot into hot sterilised jars and refrigerated after opening. Never dip a used spoon, bread or suya into a jar of sauce or pickles. Saliva and food crumbs carry microbes into the jar. Pour or scoop out what you need with a clean spoon.

Jam turns a glut of pineapple, guava, mango or oranges into a product that keeps for months unopened. Three things make it work. **Pectin**, a natural setting substance in fruit, forms a soft gel. **Acid**, from the fruit or added lemon juice, helps the pectin set. **Sugar** ties up the water in the fruit so moulds and bacteria cannot use it, and helps the gel form. If you cut the sugar a lot, the jam no longer keeps at room temperature.

The **cold chain** is the unbroken line of cold that keeps perishable food safe from the moment it is caught, slaughtered or cooked until it is eaten. At home, the weak links are a fridge that is too warm, cooked food left out too long, and power cuts. This lesson shows you how to protect each link.
A thermometer
A cheap fridge thermometer tells you whether your fridge is really cold enough.
Know your temperatures
**Fridge:** WHO advises refrigerating cooked and perishable food promptly, preferably **below 5°C**. Buy a fridge thermometer and check it in the morning before anyone opens the door.
**Freezer:** a freezer should keep food frozen rock hard. **-18°C** is the temperature commonly recommended for home freezers.
**Room temperature:** WHO advises not leaving cooked food at room temperature for more than **2 hours**.
Setting up the fridge
Keep ready-to-eat and cooked food on the upper shelves, in covered containers.
Keep raw meat, chicken and fish on the lowest shelf, in a covered bowl or tray, so juices cannot drip onto other food. This follows the WHO key: separate raw and cooked.
Do not overpack. Cold air must move around the food.
Clean spills at once and wipe the shelves weekly.
Cooling, freezing and thawing
**Cool cooked food fast.** Divide a big pot of stew or soup into shallow containers so it cools quickly, and get it into the fridge or freezer within 2 hours of cooking.
**Freeze in meal-sized portions.** Flat bags freeze and thaw faster than deep tubs, and you only take out what you need.
**Label everything** with the food name and the date. Frozen food all looks alike after a month.
**Blanch vegetables** such as ugwu or green beans briefly in boiling water and cool them before freezing, so they keep their colour.
**Thaw safely.** WHO advises against thawing frozen food at room temperature. Move it to the fridge the night before, or thaw it in the microwave and cook it at once.
**Reheat thoroughly.** Bring soups and stews back to a full boil before serving.
When the power goes off

FoodSafety.gov, the US government food safety site, gives clear guidance for power cuts. Keep the doors closed as much as possible. A closed fridge keeps food safe for up to about **4 hours**. A **full** freezer holds its temperature for about **48 hours**, and a **half-full** freezer for about **24 hours**, if the door stays closed. Perishable food that has been at **4°C or above for more than 2 hours** should be thrown away. Frozen food can be refrozen if it **still contains ice crystals** or is at 4°C or below, though the quality may drop.
How long cold lasts in a power cut
Power goes off
Fridge: about 4 hours
Half-full freezer: about 24 hours
Full freezer: about 48 hours
Keeping doors closed and freezers full stretches the time your food stays safe.
Fill empty freezer space

A full freezer stays cold longer. Fill empty spaces with clean bottles of water. Once frozen, they act like ice blocks during an outage, and you can move a few into the fridge or a cool box to keep it cold.
Worked example: deciding after an overnight outage

For example, Kemi in Port Harcourt loses power at 8 pm. It returns at 2 pm the next day. Her fridge has cooked stew, fresh fish and a carton of fruit juice. Her freezer is about half full of chicken and blended pepper. Nobody opened either door.
Length of the outage: from 8 pm to midnight is 4 hours, and from midnight to 2 pm is 14 hours, so 4 + 14 = 18 hours.
Fridge: 18 hours is far beyond the 4-hour guide, and her thermometer reads 12°C. The cooked stew and fresh fish are perishable and have been above 4°C for many hours, so she throws them away.
Freezer: 18 hours is less than the 24-hour guide for a half-full freezer. She checks the chicken and finds it still hard with ice crystals, so it can be refrozen.
The blended pepper has ice crystals too, so it goes back in.
Next time she plans to fill the empty half of the freezer with water bottles and to cook the fish on the day she buys it.
Kemi keeps the frozen food, discards the risky fridge food without tasting it, and changes her habits to stretch future outages.
Planning your power hours

If you rely on a generator or a few grid hours, run the freezer during the longest block you can and keep the door shut at other times. Open the fridge as rarely as possible: decide what you need, open, take it, close. Before a known long outage, freeze bottles of water, move tomorrow's food to the fridge, and cook fresh fish or meat rather than holding it raw.
Keep the fridge below 5°C and check it with a thermometer.
Cool cooked food fast in shallow containers and refrigerate it within 2 hours.
Thaw in the fridge or microwave, never on the counter.
Power cut guide: fridge about 4 hours, half-full freezer about 24, full freezer about 48, doors closed.
Refreeze only food that still has ice crystals or is at 4°C or below.

Put a thermometer in your fridge and record the morning temperature for five days.
Rearrange the fridge so raw food is covered on the bottom shelf and cooked food is above.
Label and date every item in your freezer, and fill empty space with water bottles.

Dry storage and stock rotation in a home store or provisions shop
Set up a dry store that keeps out damp, heat, pests and chemicals
Rotate stock using first in first out and first expired first out
Explain the difference between best before and use by dates
Calculate how many weeks of stock you hold and spot overstock before it expires

Most food in a Nigerian home or provisions shop never sees a fridge: rice, beans, garri, flour, pasta, tins, oil, sugar, noodles, dried fish, crayfish and your own dried and bottled products. They are safe for a long time only if the store is clean, dry, cool and organised. A badly kept store loses money quietly, one expired tin and one weevil-filled bag at a time.
A woman carrying a bag of groceries
Good storage protects every item a household or shop buys, from rice to tinned tomatoes.
Rules for a good dry store
**Off the floor, away from the wall.** Keep bags and cartons on pallets, shelves or planks so air flows underneath and you can see and clean behind them.
**Cool and shaded.** Keep oils, groundnuts, chocolate and bottled products away from sunny windows, zinc roofs and the cooking area. Heat speeds rancidity and spoilage.
**Dry.** Keep away from leaking roofs, sinks and damp walls. Damp brings mould to garri, flour and grains.
**Closed containers.** Once a big bag of rice, beans or garri is opened, move it into clean containers with tight lids, so insects and rats cannot reach it.
**Chemicals apart.** Store kerosene, insecticides, detergents and bleach on a separate shelf, below and away from food, never in old food or drink bottles.
**Pest watch.** Look for droppings, gnawed bags, webbing, holes in grains and live insects. Keep the floor swept and spills cleaned the same day.

If you find insects in one bag of beans or rice, move that bag away from the rest at once, check the bags around it, and clean the shelf before restocking. Use sealed traps or a professional pest service rather than scattering rat poison or spraying insecticide near open food, and keep any poison locked away from food, children and animals.
Best before and use by
Date mark
Use by / expiry date
Safety date for perishable foods
Do not sell or eat after this date. WHO's Five Keys advise not using food beyond its expiry date
Best before
Quality date; the food is at its best until then if stored as directed
Do not sell past this date; check quality and storage instructions
Date of manufacture / production
When the food was made
Use it with the shelf life to work out the expiry
Never change a date
Covering, scratching out or reprinting a date on food is dishonest and puts customers at risk. If stock is close to its date, sell it sooner at a fair price or remove it, never relabel it.
FIFO and FEFO

**FIFO** means **first in, first out**: the stock you received first is sold or used first. **FEFO** means **first expired, first out**: the item with the earliest date goes first, even if it arrived later. FEFO is safer for anything with a date. In practice: put new stock at the **back** of the shelf and bring older or earlier-dated stock to the **front**.
Stock rotation cycle
Receive and check dates
New stock behind old
Earliest date sells first
Weekly date check
Reorder by real sales
Each week the cycle catches near-date stock before it becomes a loss.
When stock arrives, check every carton: dates, dents, swelling, tears, leaks, damp and pests. Refuse damaged items.
Write the delivery date on the carton with a marker.
Place new stock behind older stock, earliest expiry at the front.
Once a week, check dates on every shelf and list anything due within a month.
Remove any bulging, leaking, rusted or badly dented tins, and any packs with mould or insects.
Worked example: weeks of stock and an overstock warning

For example, Ada runs a provisions shop in Owerri. On her weekly check she finds 7 packs of biscuits past their best-before date, priced at about ₦300 each, and 48 packs of spaghetti whose best-before date is 3 weeks away. She sells about 12 packs of spaghetti a week.
Biscuits lost: 7 × ₦300 = ₦2,100 of stock she can no longer sell.
Spaghetti cover: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 weeks of stock, but only 3 weeks are left before the date.
At her normal speed she will sell 3 × 12 = 36 packs in time, leaving 48 − 36 = 12 packs at risk.
She moves the spaghetti to the front counter, offers it in a bundle with tomato paste, and orders no more spaghetti until the shelf is down to one week of stock.
She also cuts her biscuit order, since that line sells slower than she thought.
Ada stops a likely loss on 12 packs of spaghetti and learns to order by weekly sales, not by the size of the supplier's discount.
Mouldy groundnuts, maize and garri

Sort groundnuts and maize before storing and selling, removing mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured ones. WHO notes that staples such as maize and groundnuts can carry aflatoxins, mould poisons. Do not sell or eat mouldy portions.
Keep stock off the floor, away from walls, cool, dry and in closed containers.
Store chemicals apart from food and never in food bottles.
Use FEFO: earliest date at the front, new stock at the back.
Never sell food past its date or change a date.
Weeks of stock = stock on hand ÷ weekly sales; compare it with the time left before the date.

Choose one shelf or cupboard and take everything out.
Clean the shelf, then check each item's date and condition, removing damaged or expired items.
Put items back with the earliest dates at the front.

Once you can preserve food reliably, selling the surplus is a natural next step: dried tomato flakes, smoked fish, pickles, jam or ogi to neighbours, your church, your shop or WhatsApp customers. Selling adds three new duties: packaging that keeps the food as good as the day you made it, a label that tells the truth, and a price that covers every cost.
A woman putting up a for sale sign
Selling preserved food well starts with honest packing, labelling and pricing.

Product
Good packaging
Why
Dried tomato, vegetables, mango
Thick food-grade zip or heat-sealed bags, or glass jars

If you plan to sell packaged food beyond your immediate neighbours, for example through supermarkets, other shops or across states, it will need registration with NAFDAC, the agency that regulates packaged food in Nigeria. Check NAFDAC's guidance for small businesses before you scale up.
Setting an honest best-before date
Keep back at least three packs from a batch, stored exactly as a customer would store them.
Open and check one every week or two: look, smell, texture and taste of a pack with no warning signs.
Write down the week the quality first drops (softening, darkening, loss of crunch, any mould).
Set your best-before date well inside that time, for example at around half to two-thirds of the time it stayed good.
Repeat the test whenever you change the recipe, the packaging or the supplier.
What your price must cover
Ingredients
Packaging and labels
Fuel and transport
Your labour
Profit
Price from the bottom up: every layer must be paid before the top layer is profit.
Worked example: pricing a 100 g pack of tomato flakes

For example, Funmi from Module 2 now dries 20 kg of tomatoes a month at about ₦1,200 per kg. She knows her drying ratio is 10, so she expects 2 kg of flakes. Bags cost about ₦100 each, labels about ₦50, transport to market about ₦1,500, and she values her 6 hours of work at ₦500 an hour (approximate figures).
Transport ₦1,500. Labour 6 × ₦500 = ₦3,000.
She adds 40%: ₦1,575 × 1.4 = ₦2,205, and rounds to ₦2,250 a pack, a profit of ₦2,250 − ₦1,575 = ₦675 per pack, or 20 × ₦675 = ₦13,500 a month.
Funmi has a price that pays for her time as well as her tomatoes. If buyers in her area will only pay much less, she knows it is her costs, not her guesswork, that need to change.
Take orders before you produce

Short-life products such as ogi, soft-smoked fish and fridge pickles are safest and most profitable when you take orders by WhatsApp first and produce only what is ordered. Long-life products such as well-dried foods and jam can be made ahead in planned batches.
Keeping products safe at the point of sale
Display jars and packs in the shade, never on a hot bench in the sun or on top of a fridge or generator.
Keep fridge products (fridge pickles, soft-smoked fish, ogi) in a cool box with frozen water bottles when you take them to market, and do not display them warm for hours.
Do not open packs for tasting from stock you will sell. Make a separate tasting jar and serve with clean spoons.
When a customer pays by transfer to Opay, Moniepoint or a bank, confirm the money has arrived in your app before handing over goods.

Keep a simple record for every batch: date, quantities in, quantities out, costs, the batch code on the labels, and any customer comments. If a customer reports a problem, the record tells you which jars or packs came from the same batch so you can check them quickly.
Match packaging to the product: airtight for dried food, breathable for hard-smoked fish, sterilised glass for pickles and jam.

Know the cause
Microbes: bacteria, yeasts and moulds
Enzymes: cut yam browns, banana goes black
Air: oils and groundnuts turn rancid
Pests: weevils, cockroaches, rats
Damage: bruises and cracks let germs in
Food does not go bad by magic. Every spoiled tomato has a cause you can name.
First, microbes: tiny living bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Some can make people ill without changing how the food looks.
Second, enzymes, natural substances inside food. They make a cut yam turn brown and a banana go soft and black.
Third, air. It makes groundnuts, crayfish and palm oil smell sharp and stale. We call that rancid.
Fourth, pests, which leave droppings and eggs that carry germs.
Fifth, physical damage. A bruise lets microbes and air in, and that item spoils days before its neighbours.
The big idea
Take away what microbes need
Microbes need food, water, warmth, time, air
Drying and salting take away water
Fridge and freezer take away warmth
Vinegar and fermenting make food sour
Danger zone: 5°C to 60°C
Microbes need food, water, warmth, time and, for most of them, air. Take one away and they slow down or stop. Every method in this course does that.
Drying and salting take away water.
Refrigerating and freezing take away warmth.
Pickling and fermenting make food too sour for harmful bacteria. Sugar in jam ties up water.

The WHO Five Keys poster marks 5 to 60 degrees Celsius as the danger zone, where bacteria multiply quickly. A Nigerian kitchen afternoon sits inside it. So rice left on the stove overnight can be unsafe even when it smells fine.

Days to weeks
Refrigerated cooked food

There is no single best method. Choose by the food, how long it must keep, your power, and whether you will sell it. For days or a few weeks, the fridge, light salting or fridge pickles may be enough.

For months, you need freezing, proper drying, hard smoking or real jam. Several small hurdles together are often safer than one. And remember, no method makes bad food good again. Start fresh every time.
Before every job
Check these five keys before any preserving job. Keep hands, surfaces and tools clean. Keep raw meat and fish apart from cooked food. Boil soups and stews.
Never leave cooked food out for more than 2 hours, and never thaw frozen food at room temperature. Use safe water and fresh food.
Botulism
The hidden danger in jars and oil
Never keep low-acid food sealed or under oil at room temperature.
The bacterium grows only without air
It cannot grow below pH 4.6 (acidic food)
Low-acid: garlic, ginger, onion, pepper, fish
Oil on top does not preserve food
Weakness, blurred vision: hospital at once
Botulism is a rare but very serious illness. WHO explains that the bacterium grows only where there is no air. A sealed jar or a layer of oil shuts air out.
It will not grow in acidic food, below pH 4.6.
So the risk is low-acid food, such as garlic, ginger, onions, pepper paste without vinegar, fish and meat, sealed up at room temperature. It may look and smell normal.
Oil on top does not preserve food. Make oil mixtures in small amounts, keep them in the fridge, and use them quickly.
Tiredness, weakness, blurred vision or trouble swallowing after eating preserved food means hospital at once. And never give honey to a baby under 1 year old.
Never taste to check
Bulging lid, or liquid spurts out
Cloudiness, bubbles or slime in a clear pickle
Off or rotten smell
Mouldy or discoloured groundnuts or maize
A bulging lid means gas from microbes. Mould roots go deeper than you can see, so do not scrape it off and eat.
Slime or unexpected cloudiness, or an off smell, means spoilage. Never taste to check.
Mouldy groundnuts or maize may carry aflatoxin, a mould poison. Wrap anything suspicious in a bag, put it in a covered bin, and wash your hands.
Key points
Remember
Five causes: microbes, enzymes, air, pests, damage
Every method takes away a microbe need
Remove damaged items early
Food that smells fine can still be unsafe
No low-acid food sealed or under oil in the heat

To remember. Name the cause, then take away what microbes need. Sort out damaged items early. Food that looks and smells fine can still be unsafe. And if you are ever unsure, keep it cold, use it quickly, or throw it out.

Drying is the cheapest method in a sunny country. But careless drying gives dusty, mouldy food.
Dry on mesh trays raised off the ground, never on a mat or zinc on the floor. Cover with net against flies, dust and lizards.
Mesh lets air pass under the food, so both sides dry at once.
Keep pieces in a single layer, not touching, and cut to the same thickness so they dry together.
Bring trays in at night. Night air is damp, and food takes the water back.
Wash produce in safe water, and wash your hands and knives. A solar dryer with a clear cover and netted vents is faster and cleaner still.
Is it dry enough?
Condition the batch, then weigh it
Water drops inside the jar? Spread it out and dry it more.
Fill a clean, dry jar about two-thirds full
Close it and shake once a day for a week
Loose and dry: pack in small airtight packs
Weigh fresh and dried to know your yield
Pieces on the edge dry faster than the middle, so some may still hold water. Before long storage, condition the batch. Fill a clean, dry jar about two-thirds full.
Close it and shake it once a day for about a week. If drops of water form, or pieces stick together, spread the food out and dry it more.
If it stays loose and dry, let it cool and pack it in small airtight packs, in a cool, dark place. Check every week.
For example, Funmi in Kaduna dried 4 kg of tomatoes and got 400 g. Her drying ratio is 10, so 1 kg of dried tomato needs about 10 kg fresh. Always weigh your own batch.
Step by step
Dry-salted fish
Salting must be followed by drying, smoking or cold storage.
Very fresh fish only: clear eyes, red gills
Gut, remove gills, wash the belly cavity
Split thick fish so salt reaches the centre
Salt every surface; layer, cover, keep cool
Drain the pickle, rinse off loose salt
Dry on raised, covered racks until firm
Salt pulls water out of flesh, but slowly, from the outside in. Start with very fresh fish: bright clear eyes, red gills, firm flesh. Salt will not rescue stale fish.
Gut it, remove the gills, and wash the belly well. The gut spoils fastest.
Split thick fish, or cut deep slashes, so salt reaches the thickest part.
Rub clean salt into every surface, layer fish and salt in a covered container, and keep it in the coolest shade you have.
Drain the liquid as your tested recipe directs, and rinse off loose salt.

Dry it on raised, covered racks until firm right through. A soft, wet or pink centre, or a sour smell, means throw it away. Lightly salted fish that is not dried, smoked or kept cold is not preserved.
Hot-smoking
Soft-smoked or hard-smoked?
Soft-smoked
Treat like cooked fish
Fridge, eat within days
Hard-smoked
Dry, firm, light for its size
Keeps for weeks
Airy basket in a dry place
Hot-smoking cooks, dries and coats the fish in one process. Soft-smoked fish is moist. Treat it like cooked fish: fridge, and eat within days. Never seal it airtight at room temperature.
Hard-smoked fish keeps for weeks. Smoke slowly: gentle heat dries the surface, hotter heat cooks it through, then low heat dries it for keeping.
The flesh must be opaque right to the bone. If the centre is soft and damp, give it more time on low heat, not more fire.

Smoke safely
Dry, untreated hardwood, coconut husk or charcoal. Never plastic, tyres or painted wood.
Keep fish well above the flames. Aim for a steady smoulder, not a blaze.
Smoke outdoors with a chimney. Children away. Water or sand nearby. Cotton, not synthetic clothes.
Use only dry, untreated hardwood, coconut husk or charcoal. Plastic, tyres and treated wood release poisonous smoke that settles on the food.
Keep fish well above the flames. Burnt, charred fish carries more harmful smoke substances.
Wood smoke harms your lungs and eyes. Smoke outdoors or under an open shed, with a chimney carrying smoke away from your face. Keep children away, keep water or sand nearby, and wear cotton clothes.

Weigh before and after to know your real cost

Step by step
Making ogi
Sort out mouldy grain. Souring cannot remove aflatoxin.
Clean the grain, removing mouldy ones
Steep in safe water until it crushes easily
Sieve with safe water, keep the white liquid
Settle and sour, covered
Pour off the top water: that is ogi
In a good ferment, friendly bacteria turn sugar into acid, and that sourness makes life hard for harmful bacteria.
Start by picking out stones and mouldy grains. Mouldy maize can carry aflatoxin, and souring does not remove it.
Steep the grain in plenty of safe water in a covered bucket, until a grain crushes easily. Ogi is almost all water, so safe water matters.
Grind the soft grain, then sieve it with safe water and keep the white liquid.
Cover it and let it settle and sour. Pour off the top water. The thick white sediment is ogi. Keep it under safe water changed daily, use a clean spoon, and use it within a few days.
Check your ferment
Good ferment or throw it away?
Rotten or strong cheesy smell
Pink, black or green patches
Slime or fuzzy mould
A good ferment smells clean and pleasantly sour, is white or cream, and has clear water on top.

A rotten smell, coloured patches, slime or fuzzy mould means throw it away. Ferments that do not turn clearly sour, or that are sealed and kept warm, are risky. Do not invent fermented fish or meat products for sale.
Three pickling rules
Use vinegar of 5% acidity
Never change a tested recipe's proportions
Use pickling salt if salt is needed
In a pickle, acid is the safety line. Botulism bacteria will not grow below pH 4.6.
So use white vinegar of 5% acidity. Check the label, and never use vinegar of unknown strength.
Do not change the vinegar, water and vegetables in a tested recipe. Extra water or extra vegetables weaken the acid.
If the recipe asks for salt, use pickling salt. And wear gloves when cutting hot peppers.
Worked example
Tripling a pickle without breaking it
Unless processed by a tested method, label it: Keep refrigerated.
1 kg recipe: 600 ml vinegar, 400 ml water
Triple: 1,800 ml vinegar, 1,200 ml water
Vinegar stays 60% of the liquid
Extra litre of water: only 45%. Refused.
For example, Ese sells pickled onion and carrot beside a suya spot in Benin City. Her card for 1 kg of vegetables uses 600 ml of vinegar and 400 ml of water.
For the weekend she triples everything: 1,800 ml of vinegar and 1,200 ml of water.
Vinegar is still 60% of the liquid, so the acid strength is unchanged.

Her sister suggests an extra litre of water to stretch it. Ese refuses, because the vinegar would fall to 45%. She fills hot sterilised jars, boiled fully covered for 10 minutes, and keeps them in the fridge.
Jam that sets and keeps
Surface wrinkles on a cold saucer? The jam is ready.
Weigh prepared fruit; chill a few saucers
Cook fruit soft; add lemon if low in pectin
Dissolve every sugar crystal on low heat
Boil hard, stirring often
Test on a cold saucer
Hot-fill hot sterilised jars, wipe rims, close

Jam works through three things. Pectin, a natural setting substance in fruit, forms the gel. Acid helps it set. Sugar ties up water so moulds cannot use it. Weigh your fruit and put a few saucers in the freezer.
Cook the fruit soft. Pineapple and mango are low in pectin, so add lemon juice, or some guava or citrus.
Add the recipe's sugar and stir on low heat until every crystal dissolves, or the jam turns grainy.
Boil hard, stirring. Then drop a little on a cold saucer, wait a minute and push it. If it wrinkles, it is ready. If it runs, boil a few minutes more.
Pour it into hot sterilised jars, wipe the rims, close at once and label.
Safety
Hot sugar, open jars, mould
Hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Deep pot half full, long spoon, children away.
Keep it covered in the fridge and use a clean, dry spoon every time.
Throw away the whole jar. Mould threads grow below the surface you can see.
Boiling sugar is much hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Use a deep pot no more than half full and a long wooden spoon, and keep children away.
After opening, keep jars in the fridge, and never dip a used spoon, bread or suya into the jar.
Mould on jam means the whole jar goes in the bin. Do not scrape the top and eat the rest.

Cold storage, shop shelves and selling honestly
Cold storage, shop shelves, and selling honestly.
This is the video for module 4 of Food Preservation and Storage.
The cold chain
Fridge: below 5°C, checked with a thermometer
Freezer: -18°C, food frozen rock hard
Cooked food out: no more than 2 hours
Raw meat and fish on the lowest shelf
The cold chain is the unbroken line of cold from market or pot to plate. Keep your fridge below 5 degrees Celsius. Check it with a thermometer in the morning, before anyone opens the door.
A home freezer should be at about minus 18 degrees, with food frozen rock hard.
Never leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
Keep raw meat, chicken and fish covered on the lowest shelf, so juices cannot drip onto cooked food.
Step by step
Cool, freeze, thaw, reheat
Never thaw frozen food on the counter.
Cool stew fast in shallow containers
Freeze flat, meal-sized portions
Label every bag with name and date
Thaw in the fridge overnight
Reheat to a full boil
Divide a big pot of stew into shallow containers so it cools quickly, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours.
Freeze in flat, meal-sized bags. They freeze and thaw faster, and you take out only what you need.
Label every bag. Frozen food all looks alike after a month.
Move frozen food to the fridge the night before. Never thaw it at room temperature.
Bring soups and stews back to a full boil before serving.
Doors closed
Safe for up to about 4 hours with the door closed.
Holds for about 24 hours. A full freezer holds for about 48 hours.
Perishables at 4°C or above for over 2 hours: throw out. Ice crystals left: can refreeze.
In a power cut, keep the doors closed. A closed fridge keeps food safe for up to about 4 hours.
A half-full freezer holds for about 24 hours, and a full one about 48. So fill empty space with bottles of water. Once frozen, they act like ice blocks.
Perishable food at 4 degrees or above for more than 2 hours goes in the bin, without tasting. Frozen food that still has ice crystals can be refrozen.
Worked example
Deciding after an 18-hour outage
Power off 8 pm to 2 pm: 18 hours
Fridge at 12°C: stew and fish thrown away
Freezer: under 24 hours, ice crystals: keep
Next time: water bottles in the freezer
For example, Kemi in Port Harcourt loses power from 8 pm until 2 pm the next day. That is 18 hours, and nobody opened the doors.
Her fridge reads 12 degrees, far beyond the 4-hour guide. She throws away the cooked stew and fresh fish.
Her half-full freezer was off for less than 24 hours, and the chicken still has ice crystals, so it goes back in.
Next time she will fill the freezer with water bottles and cook fish the day she buys it.
Dry store and shop
Rotate stock: first expired, first out
Never sell food past its date, and never change a date.
Off the floor, away from walls, cool and dry
Chemicals on a separate shelf, below food
Check dates, dents and pests on arrival
New stock at the back, earliest date in front
Weekly check: list anything due within a month
Keep bags on shelves or pallets, off the floor and away from walls, in a cool, dry place. Move opened rice, beans or garri into containers with tight lids.
Store kerosene, insecticide and bleach on a separate shelf, below food, and never in old food bottles.
When stock arrives, check dates, dents, swelling, leaks and pests. Refuse damaged items.
Use FEFO, first expired, first out. Put new stock at the back and the earliest date at the front.
Once a week, check every shelf. For example, Ada in Owerri found 48 packs of spaghetti but sells only 12 a week, with 3 weeks to the date. She moved them to the front counter and stopped ordering.
Covering or changing a date is dishonest and puts customers at risk.
Tell the truth
Product name that says what it is
Ingredients, largest amount first
Net weight or volume
Date made and best-before date
Storage instructions
Your business name and phone number
